Unstressed syllables (often referred to as “minor syllables” in Southeast Asian linguistics) cannot occur on a right word edge and consist of only an initial consonant plus a brief schwa vowel (Cə̆). [p. 25] ... This observation concerning Khmer applies equally well across Southeast Asia languages, including Asho Chin. Looking at Southeast Asian languages from several families, Butler (2015:449) analyzed sesquisyllables as disyllables with “word-final prosodic prominence and phonological reduction of the penultimate syllable.” ... new_statements.quote: Minor syllables cannot occur on the right word edge (and thus cannot stand alone), but must be followed by a major syllable. [...] 5.3.1 Iambic weakening. Asho Chin has an iambic stress pattern, and the Iambic/Trochaic Law (Hayes 1995:79–85) predicts that iambic languages will either lengthen stressed syllables or shorten unstressed syllables in order to increase the durational contrast within a foot. Asho (like most Southeast Asian languages) chooses to reduce unstressed syllables, and it is this process that often generates the frequent minor syllables. [...] Syllables that undergo weakening lose vowel place features, coda consonants, and tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Asho Chin is a two-tone (H/L) sesquisyllabic language with iambic word prosody: words are (minor)+major; the minor syllable (Cə̆) is unstressed and toneless and may never be word-final, the major (full) syllable is stressed, so stress falls on the final syllable of the (sesqui/di-syllabic) word; in compounds the first monosyllabic member may weaken to an unstressed minor syllable in casual speech. Tignor explicitly equates 'minor syllable' with 'unstressed syllable' and 'major' with 'stressed' (p. 60), adopting Butler's (2015) 'word-final prosodic prominence' analysis for Asho.
new_statements.exceptions: Iambic weakening of compound first members is 'inconsistent' and more common in fast/casual speech; high-tone syllables reduced to minor syllables 'often retained a high pitch' (p. 69); Plains-dialect speaker replaces the Hill syllabic nasal with unstressed /ʔə̆/.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical words and noun compounds, elicited citation forms from two speakers in Yangon, 2015); tone (H vs L) is contrastive only on stressed/major syllables (p. 25: two tones 'which can occur with both open and closed stressed syllables').
new_statements.identity_note: Tignor 2018 describes the Hill ('Kone-tu') dialect of Asho Chin proper [csh], Myanmar (consultant from Ngape Township, Magway Region), with comparative notes on the Plains ('Ok-tu') dialect (Daik-U Township, Bago Region); this is squarely asho1236. Zakaria 2018 (the Glottolog 'grammar' for asho1236) describes Laitu Hyow (exonym Khyang) of Gungrupara, Bandarban, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh -- corresponding to Glottolog's 'Chittagong' dialect chit1280 under asho1236, though the variety name 'Laitu' overlaps with Laitu Chin [clj] lait1239 of Rakhine State; Zakaria treats Hyow as a Southern Chin language coordinate with Asho (Peterson 2017 'Hyow/Asho'). The two sources differ: Tignor gives Asho an iambic (final) stress pattern over a two-tone system; Zakaria states Hyow uses only tone and intonation suprasegmentally (three tones, almost no sesquisyllables).

sources.note: Asho is sesquisyllabic with two level tones (H, L) on major syllables; minor syllables (Cə̆) are unstressed, cannot be word-final and must be followed by a major (stressed) syllable; 'Asho Chin has an iambic stress pattern' (p. 69, sec. 5.3.1); unstressed syllables reduce (lose vowel place, coda and tone); Butler/Hayes analysis of word-final prominence adopted for Asho (p. 60).

sources.note: Sec. 2.6 (p. 73): 'Hyow utilize only tone and intonation as suprasegmental features' -- i.e. no word stress is described; three lexical tones (H, L, Falling) plus grammatical tone; only two sesquisyllabic words in the language (p. c. 2155 of txt). Variety = Laitu Hyow of Gungrupara, Bandarban, Bangladesh.
